Image:alt: A giraffe stands tall in a savanna landscape.
Hint 1: My tongue can be almost 50 cm long.
Hint 2: I have a one-of-a-kind spot pattern.
Hint 3: I’m the tallest land animal on Earth.
Fun Facts: A giraffe’s heart can weigh more than 10 kilograms, and it pumps blood all the way up its long neck.

Image:alt: A red panda rests on a wooden platform, showing its reddish coat and bushy tail.
Hint 1: I spend most of my day curled up asleep in a tree.
Hint 2: My diet is almost entirely bamboo, even though I'm not closely related to the black-and-white panda.
Hint 3: I have a bushy ringed tail and a reddish coat, and people sometimes call me a 'red cat-bear.'
Fun Facts: Red pandas use their bushy tails as blankets in cold weather and have a false thumb, an extended wrist bone, that helps them grip bamboo stems.
Image Attribution: Photo: Bernard Landgraf, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A pale, gelatinous blobfish with a droopy, saggy face.
Hint 1: I live so deep underwater that the pressure would crush most other fish.
Hint 2: Out of the water, gravity makes me look nothing like I do in my natural habitat.
Hint 3: I've been voted one of the world's ugliest animals, and my saggy face is famous online.
Fun Facts: A blobfish's body is mostly a gel-like substance slightly less dense than water, letting it float just above the sea floor without wasting energy swimming.
Image Attribution: Photo: Alphama, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Aliases: scaly anteater, Sunda pangolin, Manis javanica
Image:alt: A scaly pangolin walking across the forest floor.
Hint 1: I'm the only mammal in the world completely covered in scales.
Hint 2: When I feel threatened, I roll up into a tight, armored ball.
Hint 3: I use a long, sticky tongue to slurp up ants and termites, much like an anteater.
Fun Facts: A pangolin's tongue can be longer than its own body, and it retracts into a pouch near its pelvis when not in use.
Image Attribution: Photo: Ari hidayat99, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Aliases: unicorn of the sea, Monodon monoceros
Image:alt: An old illustration of a narwhal showing its long, spiraled tusk.
Hint 1: I live year-round in cold Arctic waters.
Hint 2: Males of my species usually grow a single long, spiraled tusk.
Hint 3: That tusk is actually an overgrown tooth, and it's inspired centuries of unicorn legends.
Fun Facts: A narwhal's tusk is a canine tooth that can grow up to 3 meters long and is packed with nerve endings, possibly helping it sense changes in the water.
Image Attribution: Photo: The Public Domain Review, Public Domain, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A platypus being held near a riverbank, showing its duck-like bill.
Hint 1: I lay eggs, even though I'm a mammal.
Hint 2: I have a soft, sensitive bill that I use to detect prey underwater.
Hint 3: I look like a mix of a duck, a beaver, and an otter, and the males among us have a venomous spur on their hind legs.
Fun Facts: When platypuses were first described to European scientists, many believed the pelt was an elaborate hoax stitched together from other animals.
Image Attribution: Photo: TwoWings, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A pale pink axolotl with feathery external gills, resting underwater.
Hint 1: I never really grow up, I keep my juvenile features my whole life.
Hint 2: If I lose a limb, or even part of my heart or brain, I can regrow it.
Hint 3: I'm a salamander with feathery external gills and a face that always looks like it's smiling.
Fun Facts: Axolotls are critically endangered in the wild in Mexico, even though they're one of the most common amphibians kept in captivity worldwide.
Image Attribution: Photo: Marius Maehlen (Mariblubb), CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A chameleon gripping a branch with its curled tail and independently rotating eyes.
Hint 1: Each of my eyes can swivel and focus independently of the other.
Hint 2: I'm famous for changing color, though it's more about mood and temperature than blending in.
Hint 3: I have a long, sticky tongue I can shoot out faster than a blink to catch insects.
Fun Facts: A chameleon's tongue can extend to more than one and a half times its own body length and accelerates faster than a fighter jet.
Image Attribution: Photo: Zeynel Cebeci, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Aliases: three-toed sloth, brown-throated sloth, Bradypus variegatus
Image:alt: A sloth hanging from a tree branch, moving slowly through the canopy.
Hint 1: I move so slowly that algae grows in my fur.
Hint 2: I spend almost my entire life hanging upside down in trees.
Hint 3: I'm famous as one of the slowest-moving mammals on Earth.
Fun Facts: Sloths only leave their trees to go to the bathroom about once a week, and the trip can be dangerous since it's when they're most vulnerable to predators.
Image Attribution: Photo: Krunal Desai, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A seahorse floating upright in the water, its tail curled around a strand of seagrass.
Hint 1: In my species, it's the males who carry the babies, not the females.
Hint 2: I swim upright, and I'm a famously weak swimmer despite living in the open ocean.
Hint 3: My head looks like a horse's, which is exactly how I got my name.
Fun Facts: Male seahorses carry fertilized eggs in a specialized pouch and give birth to fully-formed babies, one of the only examples of male pregnancy in the animal kingdom.
Image Attribution: Photo: FASTILY, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: An octopus crawling across the seafloor, its arms spread across the rocks.
Hint 1: I have three hearts and blue blood.
Hint 2: I can squeeze my entire boneless body through any gap bigger than my beak.
Hint 3: I have eight arms lined with suckers, and I'm famous for being one of the smartest invertebrates alive.
Fun Facts: An octopus can change both the color and texture of its skin in less than a second to blend almost perfectly into its surroundings.
Image Attribution: Photo: Martijn Klijnstra, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A bright pink flamingo standing on one leg in shallow water.
Hint 1: The pink or reddish color of my feathers actually comes from what I eat.
Hint 2: I usually stand and sleep balanced on just one leg.
Hint 3: I'm known for my long legs, curved neck, and bright pink feathers, and I usually live in large flocks.
Fun Facts: Flamingos get their pink color from pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat, and in captivity they can turn pale without the right diet.
Image Attribution: Photo: Charles J. Sharp, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A close-up of a monarch butterfly's orange and black wings.
Hint 1: I make one of the longest migrations of any insect on Earth.
Hint 2: My caterpillar stage eats almost nothing but milkweed, which makes me toxic to most predators.
Hint 3: I'm an orange-and-black butterfly, and no single one of us completes the whole migration round trip, it takes multiple generations.
Fun Facts: Monarch butterflies that migrate south in the fall can live up to 8 months, far longer than the few weeks a typical summer generation survives.
Image Attribution: Photo: Charles Patrick Ewing, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A koala climbing a eucalyptus tree trunk.
Hint 1: I sleep around 20 hours a day.
Hint 2: My diet is almost entirely eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic to most other animals.
Hint 3: I'm a tree-dwelling marsupial from Australia, often mistaken for a bear, even though I'm not one.
Fun Facts: Koalas have fingerprints so similar to human fingerprints that they can be difficult to tell apart even under a microscope.
Image Attribution: Photo: Diliff (David Iliff), CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons
